conclusion.justification: The report concludes that available evidence does not support the claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism, citing multiple large studies and expert consensus finding no association.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion:** The available evidence does not support the claim that giving children a greater number of vaccines causes autism.

The concern partly arose from a 1998 report involving only 12 children; subsequent investigation found major problems, and the paper was retracted. That type of small, uncontrolled observation cannot establish causation. https://www.webmd.com/brain/autism/do-vaccines-cause-autism

More relevant research has tested vaccine exposure directly. A 2013 case-control study compared 256 children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) with 752 controls, using vaccine registries and medical records to assess total exposure to vaccine antibody-stimulating proteins and polysaccharides. Its reported conclusion was that increased exposure was **not associated** with autism risk. https://gutsandgrowth.com/2013/08/21/too-many-vaccines-and-autism-is-debunked/

Evidence also addresses proposed ingredients rather than merely the number of injections. A nationwide Danish cohort of more than 1.2 million children found no association between aluminum-adsorbed vaccine exposure and neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2837599

For MMR specifically, the World Health Organization’s vaccine-safety committee concluded that no evidence supports a causal association with autism or autistic disorders. https://www.who.int/groups/global-advisory-committee-on-vaccine-safety/topics/mmr-vaccines-and-autism

These studies cannot prove that autism never occurs after vaccination—many diagnoses naturally occur during the same childhood period—but they do not find the increased risk predicted by the claim.
